expectations.text: The drafted variants make genuinely different arguments rather than rewording one claim.
expectations.evidence: Three distinct argument families are drafted and labelled in the angle bank — pain (nightly decision fatigue), mechanism/speed (one 10-minute sit-down replaces daily decisions), and price-value ($4.99/mo) — each doubled across a different awareness stage, with differing formulas (PAS, 4 Us, mechanism-led, symptom-led, BAB, offer-led). The price-value rows argue cost ('Less than one takeout order, all month'), clearly separate from the pain rows' takeout-loop framing, and mechanism_sa uniquely explains how it works ('answer a few quick questions'). expectations.text: Any drafted variants keep message match with the landing page promise of planning a week of meals in 10 minutes.
expectations.evidence: Five of six variants state both halves of the promise explicitly ("your full week, planned in 10 minutes, for $4.99/month", "literally 10 minutes, start to finish", "10 minutes, one week sorted", "Your week, planned in 10 minutes", "Plan your whole week of meals in 10 minutes"). Variant 3 ("Plan 7 days of meals in the time it takes to make coffee") keeps the week but substitutes a vaguer, arguably faster-than-10-minutes benchmark, a minor drift from the exact landing-page claim.

expectations.text: The drafted variants make genuinely different arguments rather than rewording one claim.
expectations.evidence: All six restate the same core speed claim (10 minutes / one week) with varied metaphors rather than distinct arguments. Only two secondary angles appear: price ($4.99 in #2 and #6) and decision fatigue (#1 "no decision fatigue", #3 "stop staring at your fridge", #6 "never ask 'what's for dinner'"). Variants 4 and 5 add nothing beyond a rephrasing of speed ("literally 10 minutes, start to finish" vs "less time than deciding what to watch tonight"), and no variant argues from cost-of-groceries, waste reduction, nutrition, family/household fit, or any other independent benefit.
